newsitem.title: USA: Acordia tests market for brokerage sale.
newsitem.headline: Acordia tests market for brokerage sale.

text.p: Acordia Inc is testing the waters for the possible sale of its property and casualty brokerage business, but analysts said it may be hard to find a buyer.

"It's a business that is not terribly profitable," said Robinson-Humphrey analyst Thomas Rosencrants. "The property casualty business remains intensely competitive, and a 10-year price war in commercial lines remains very much in place."
Acordia property and casualty brokerage operations had revenues of $335 million in 1996.
Rosencrants said he would be surprised if the property/casualty brokerage business garnered any material premium over the current stock price.
Ira Zuckerman, an analyst with Nutmeg Securities Ltd, agrees. "I would not expect (a price of) any more than one times revenues," he said.
The Indianapolis-based company's 1996 revenues were $661 million, including revenues from its managed healthcare and consulting services businesses.
Acordia is at a crossroads, analysts said, following last week's announcement by major shareholder Anthem Insurance Cos Inc that Acordia may no longer fit its business plan.

Anthem, which holds 67 percent of Acordia, has hired Credit Suisse First Boston to assist it in exploring the possible sale of Acordia's property and casualty brokerage business and possible reorganization of Acordia's health business.

Acordia, which was started by Anthem, completed its initial public offering in 1992. Last week Anthem, a mutual insurance company that provides health insurance and managed health care, said Acordia's property and casualty business and relationship between the two companies may no longer be consistent with Anthem's mission.

Acordia derives about 44 percent of its revenues by providing claims administration and sales and marketing services to Anthem. The balance come from its insurance brokerage operations, which focuses primarily on property and casualty.
Acordia management said it is projecting revenues from health-related operations will be flat to slightly down in 1997 compared to 1996.

Asked about the company's future without its property and casualty brokerage business, Acordia chief financial officer Keith Maib told Reuters, "We're going through the evaluation process, and we'll decide those issues as we work through them."
Maib said Acordia's strategic review may take some time.
"We hope to work through the evaluation process in 1997," he said, declining to comment whether there were any early expressions of interest for the property and casualty business.
Acordia's board has created a special committee of independent members who are not affiliated with Anthem or Acordia management to evaluate any proposals either made by or involving Anthem.
In 1996, Acordia earned $2.09 a share versus $1.64 the prior year.
